book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts

chapters.file: ch03 - The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series.md

chapters.relation: The editor, invoking Plato's claim that philosophy begins in wonder, argues that Rowling like Tolkien and Lewis deliberately poses serious philosophical questions for young readers. He frames the volume's agenda through the books' own material: whether love is the most powerful magic, whether souls exist and can be split by Voldemort's Horcruxes, what Animagi and boggarts teach about personal identity, whether a love potion could ever be ethically used, whether Kingsley's 'every human life is worth the same' is true, and whether Dumbledore is right that something can be real even if it exists only inside one's head. It explains the book covers the complete seven-novel saga with emphasis on the final two volumes.

chapters.file: ch10 - PART ONE - THE HORCRUX OF THE MATTER DESTINY, IDENTITY, AND THE SOUL.md
ch11 - Philosophical Conceptions of the Soul.md
chapters.relation: Scott Sehon opens his chapter by cataloguing how central souls are to the plot: Harry, Sirius, and Dudley narrowly escape dementors while Barty Crouch Jr. does not, and Voldemort's Horcruxes split his soul into eight parts that must all be destroyed before he can die. He sets up the guiding question of what the soul is in Rowling's world, where souls generally survive bodily death, and announces a survey of philosophical accounts to test whether her picture is plausible.

Presents the life-source view held by some ancient Greek philosophers, on which the soul simply accounts for life itself, so that all living things, plants and animals alike, are ensouled. It applies the view to Rowling's world by noting that Blast-Ended Skrewts and even gillyweed would then have souls, though few philosophers today accept this conception.

Presents the sentience view, on which the soul is responsible for the capacity to feel pleasure and pain and for all higher-level thought, excluding plants but not sentient animals. It notes the view would oddly grant souls even to the Whomping Willow within Rowling's universe, since magical plants there display direct sensation.

Explains Descartes' narrowing of the soul to higher cognition: sensation can be accounted for materially, but language and complex belief require an immaterial soul, so nonhuman animals are soulless. It shows how magical creatures complicate this in Rowling's world, since owls seem to understand speech and Crookshanks seems abnormally intelligent, and notes that the first three views all treat the soul as an immaterial substance able to survive death, motivating the materialist alternative.

Defines materialism as the view that nothing exists but matter and physical forces, so all mental life is brain process, there is no soul, and death is simply the end. This is the position the chapter will measure against the Potter world, where souls demonstrably survive bodily death.

Distinguishes the everyday sentimental use of 'soul', from Hoagy Carmichael's 'Heart and Soul' to soul mates and soulful art, arguing such talk is metaphorical commentary on our deepest emotions, love, and conscience that even materialists need not renounce. It foreshadows the chapter's conclusion that Rowling's conception of the soul mixes this sentimental view with a metaphysics drawn from the sentience and Cartesian views.

Argues materialism is straightforwardly false within the Potter universe, using Hermione's claim that a sword through the body leaves the soul untouched, and then taxonomizes the forms surviving souls take: Nearly Headless Nick's explanation that ghosts are imprints of wizards who refused to 'go on', Voldemort's bodiless state as 'less than the meanest ghost' after his curse rebounded on baby Harry, the graveyard echo in Goblet of Fire where Cedric and Harry's parents emerge 'more solid' than ghosts, and the Resurrection Stone in Deathly Hallows returning Sirius, Lupin, and his parents as 'neither ghost nor truly flesh'.

Uses Lupin's account of the Dementor's Kiss, whose victims like Barty Crouch Jr. go on existing as empty shells without memory or self, to eliminate the leading views of the soul: the soul cannot be the source of life, of sentience, or even of Cartesian higher thought, since the soulless victim may still sense and think dimly. The chapter compares the Kiss's aftermath to severe dementia or to Lockhart after his backfired memory charm, raising the question of whether the person rather than just the body survives.

Reconstructs Slughorn's lesson to young Tom Riddle, that murder rips the soul and the torn piece can be hidden in a Horcrux, an act 'against nature', and argues that because Voldemort's intellect and magical powers remain intact while his capacity to charm gives way to rule by fear and his body becomes snake-like, Rowling's soul must be the sentimental one: our humanity, love, and moral conscience. On this view the soul is damaged by supreme evil and can be repaired only through remorse, which is exactly what Harry urges on Voldemort ('be a man... try for some remorse') before the final killing curse rebounds.

Steps outside the fiction to ask whether Rowling's hybrid soul theory is actually plausible, answering probably not: neuroscience shows no brain events lacking physical cause, mind-body interaction remains the classic obstacle for any dualism, and it is doubly implausible that an immaterial substance would be responsible only for our deepest emotions and conscience. The differing physical powers of ghosts, Resurrection Stone shades, and Horcrux-souls make the metaphysics even harder, though the chapter concedes that a fictional soul picture that vividly dramatizes what we care about needs no truth to make a terrific story.

Eric Saidel launches his chapter from a puzzle: why would Sirius, outside for the first time in months, celebrate by chasing his tail in Order of the Phoenix? He asks whether an Animagus is a man in a dog's body, a dog in a man's body, or a third thing, and extends the question to Pettigrew, Rita Skeeter, McGonagall, werewolf Lupin, boggarts, and Polyjuice transformations such as Barty Crouch Jr.'s eerily effective impersonation of Moody.

Tests the Cartesian division of the transformed Padfoot into mind plus body across four possible combinations and rejects them all: Sirius's human body cannot plausibly slip 'into non-being' during transformation (against McGonagall's quip), yet a Sirius-mind cannot explain tail-chasing and a dog-mind cannot explain Padfoot standing on his hind legs to embrace Harry at King's Cross. Mind-body dualism thus fails as an account of what the transformed person is.

chapters.file: ch25 - A Step in the Right Direction.md
chapters.relation: Recasts the puzzle as a question of whose reasons cause the transformed person's actions, then shows this framing fails too: Polyjuice victims act on their own reasons, since Harry-as-Runcorn warns Arthur Weasley and strips Umbridge's door while Ron-as-Cattermole ignores the wife his host would protect, dogs chase tails because it feels good rather than for reasons, and werewolf Lupin attacks from instinct rather than acquiring a reason to harm his students.

Proposes that some of Padfoot's behavior is explained by his dog's body rather than Sirius's mind, imagined through a counterfactual in which Sirius became a bear instead and would never have chased his tail. But the strategy generates absurd costs: if tail-chasing feels good, it is unclear whether the feeling belongs to Sirius's mind or to the dog's body, forcing the strange conclusion that a person's body might have reasons of its own that clash with the person's will.

Concludes that transformed persons are unified mind-body wholes rather than pilot-and-ship pairings, enlisting Descartes himself, who insisted he is 'not only lodged in my body, like a pilot in his ship' but compounded with it into a single whole. The evidence is textual: Polyjuiced Harry naturally 'thunders' with Runcorn's powerful frame while acting for Harry's reasons, Luna recognizes Harry through Barny Weasley's facial expression, and Crouch-as-Moody makes sense as an indivisible embodiment, so Padfoot is neither man nor dog but a third kind of being, a man-dog.

Jeremy Pierce contrasts Trelawney's fraudulent fortune-telling, tea leaves, tarot, crystal balls, and her endlessly repeated predictions of Harry's death, with the two 'real predictions' even Dumbledore certifies. Using McGonagall's dismissal of divination and Firenze's distinction between Seers and 'the self-flattering nonsense humans call fortune-telling', the section poses the chapter's question: what makes a prophecy genuine?

Credits Aristotle with first raising whether the future is fixed and builds a sevenfold taxonomy of how a Seer might access the future, from fallible sensory prediction like Trelawney's and Muggle weather reports, through glimpses of likely or possible futures as Dumbledore describes, to infallible access to a deterministic or actual future. The section then asks which kind Trelawney's two genuine prophecies are.

Reads Dumbledore's gloss on the prophecy, 'you are free to choose your way, quite free to turn your back on the prophecy', as treating even real prophecies as non-compelling, and argues the two true prophecies cannot be mere likelihoods because they are involuntary trances with a magical source. Trelawney's card-reading episodes in Half-Blood Prince, accurate while she is oblivious to Harry behind the statue and to the lightning-struck tower, hint at inconsistent unconscious access to the future.

Examines Dumbledore's suggestion that the first prophecy was self-fulfilling: it did not originally mean Harry rather than Neville, but Voldemort's choice of the half-blood he saw himself in marked Harry as his equal, and Snape's ejection from the interview left Voldemort ignorant of the risk that attacking Harry would transfer power to him. Invoking Alexander of Aphrodisias's discussion of the Oedipus prophecy, the section argues a genuine prophecy reveals rather than causes the future, so self-fulfillment cannot distinguish Trelawney's real predictions, since the prophecy never made Voldemort do anything.

Takes Rowling's 2007 remark that there is 'no such thing as destiny' and maps the logical space it could occupy: compatibilist freedom within a predetermined course, libertarian freedom with a fixed future of true statements about what will happen, or an open future where claims about free choices are neither true nor false until made. The section asks whether Dumbledore means prophecies do not compel anyone or that their content is merely one of several possible futures.

chapters.file: ch34 - Time Travel and Fixed Time.md
chapters.relation: Argues Trelawney's second prophecy, that the servant will break free and rejoin the Dark Lord that very night, was far too improbable to be a merely likely prediction given how easily Wormtail's escape could have failed. Likewise the chain running from the first prophecy through Wormtail becoming Secret-Keeper to Lily's protective sacrifice shows the 'real' prophecies need a stronger connection to the actual future than probability.

Defends a fixed-time theory from the Prisoner of Azkaban time-travel episode, where later-Harry casts the stag Patronus that saved earlier-Harry and Buckbeak and Sirius are saved without anything changing, while acknowledging Hermione's warnings about wizards killing their past selves complicate the picture, and adds special relativity's absence of an absolute present as further support. The section then argues that the sheer improbability of the luck fulfilling the prophecies, the Myrtle's-bathroom Polyjuice chain, Felix Felicis, the capture that delivers Griphook, and Harry's arrival at the Shrieking Shack, makes better sense with something like divine providence guiding events than with pure chance.

chapters.file: ch37 - PART TWO - THE MOST POWERFUL MAGIC OF ALL.md
ch38 - Snape and the Many-Splendored Thing.md
chapters.relation: Catherine Jack Deavel and David Paul Deavel open with the puzzle of Dumbledore's 'ironclad' certainty about Snape, maintained even after Snape kills him and attested by McGonagall's report that his repentance was 'absolutely genuine'. Their answer is Snape's unrequited love for Lily Potter, and they set the chapter's task: to examine, against the suspicion that redemptive love-talk is mere sentimentality, what philosophers have said about love's nature and its power to transform and to mislead judgment.

Surveys the classical triad of eros, philia, and agape from Plato's Symposium onward and maps it onto the series: the Weasleys, Ron and Hermione, and Harry and Ginny exemplify romantic love, Dumbledore's remark that Voldemort never had a friend dramatizes the absence of philia, and Lily's self-giving love that repels Quirrell and Voldemort is agape. Because traditional accounts treat love as an act of the will rather than a feeling, Snape's persistent dislikes cannot disprove that his love for Lily has transformed him.

Traces how Snape shares the abandoned-boys origin of both Harry and Voldemort, a mixed bloodline and a feuding home that made Hogwarts the first real home for all three, 'the Half-Blood Prince' title itself an attempt to bury his Muggle ancestry. Where Voldemort chose power, selfishness, and a fragmented psyche and Harry opened himself to friends, the section frames the question of what makes the third lost boy, Dumbledore's double agent and killer, tick.

Defines love, with Aristotle, Aquinas, and M. Scott Peck, as willing the good of the other for the other's own sake, and reads Snape's double-agent life as love expressed in action despite real hatred: he protects Harry's enemies at constant risk while disliking most of them. His Occlumency, the skill to lie to Voldemort's face, reveals both strength and weakness, for rather than renouncing love as Voldemort did he only conceals it, and his dying gift of memories to Harry, revealing that Harry is a Horcrux, must be freely offered because his thoughts can never be taken.

Reads Snape's love for Lily through Plato's Symposium: his childhood watching of Lily with 'undisguised greed', his failure to ask Voldemort to spare her husband and child, 'You disgust me', shows a love that desires Lily's good only as it relates to him, falling short of Aristotle's beloved as 'second self'. Diotima's 'possession of the good forever' and 'giving birth in beauty' describe how his love matures into genuine virtue, a deepening Pope Benedict XVI's picture of love as 'ecstasy', an exodus out of the closed self toward self-giving, completes.

Argues Snape's redemption is gradual virtue-building rather than instant transformation, since vice and virtue are habits built up over time and his resentments persist even as his actions serve the good. His doe Patronus, matching Lily's, manifests Aristotle's beloved as a second self, his remorse, an emotion he shares with Harry but Voldemort cannot feel, begins to knit his damaged soul whole, and Harry's forgiveness, naming his son Albus Severus for 'the bravest man I ever knew', completes the arc love began.

Gregory Bassham opens by contrasting Muggle spending on attractiveness with the wizarding world's far more reliable magical love potions, and poses the ethical problem of their nonconsensual use. The chapter's test cases are the two key episodes: Merope Gaunt's use of a love potion to ensnare Tom Riddle Sr., Voldemort's father, and her eventual choice to stop dosing him at great cost to herself and her unborn son.

Catalogues what Half-Blood Prince establishes about love potions: Fred and George sell them legally at Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes, Hermione identifies Amortentia by its mother-of-pearl sheen and personal smell, and Slughorn warns it 'doesn't really create love... It is impossible to manufacture or imitate love', producing only obsessive infatuation, as Ron's Romilda Vane episode demonstrates. The section ends by introducing Voldemort's mother as the person who actually used one.

chapters.file: ch47 - Real Love or Mere Infatuation.md
chapters.relation: Retells Dumbledore's reconstruction of Merope Gaunt's ensnarement of Tom Riddle Sr.: Harry correctly narrows the cause of the squire's son's behavior to the Imperius Curse or a love potion, and Dumbledore concludes she dosed him, then chose to stop, wrongly hoping he had come to love her or would stay for the baby. The section closes on Dumbledore's insistence that this backstory 'has everything to do with the prophecy' about Harry and Voldemort.

Argues Merope did not truly love Riddle because the potion robbed him of the freedom to do otherwise, invoking Harry Frankfurt's denial that alternative possibilities are necessary for freedom and noting that even compatibilists deny potion-induced affection is free, since Tom would not have wanted to love her under magical inducement. Real love respects the beloved's true interests and creates a relationship in which both grow, and even self-administered potions wrong the user by forfeiting the moral growth that only uncoerced commitment makes possible.

Contends that Voldemort was not his mother's son: what defines a person is the habitual pattern of choices, as in Aristotle's 'we are what we consistently do', and Merope, who freed Riddle at the cost of her own life and renounced magic entirely, is a genuine though partial redemption, whereas Voldemort followed Marvolo Gaunt and Salazar Slytherin instead. Quoting William Hasker on how love potions trap both parties because love must be freely bestowed, the section argues character is destiny only if forged by free choice, and that Harry, protected by his mother's sacrificial love, shows what Voldemort's rejection of love and vulnerability destroyed.

chapters.file: ch51 - The Feminist Debate So Far.md
chapters.relation: Anne Collins Smith announces the chapter's thesis: in Rowling's universe love crosses hierarchical boundaries and defeats evil most effectively precisely when it does not compete, as self-sacrifice and kindness overwhelm greed and ambition without fighting them on their own terms. She claims this pattern resonates with radical feminism, and sets up a survey of feminist scholarship on Harry Potter before examining love's role in the books.

Surveys the divided feminist reception of the series: Schoefer, Heilman, and Dresang charge it with reinforcing gender stereotypes, from giggling girls to the absence of any woman as heroic as Harry or wise as Dumbledore, while Kern, Zettel, and Gladstein defend it on contextual grounds, Lavender's silliness mirroring Dean and Seamus, Trelawney mirroring Lockhart, and Umbridge and Bellatrix commanding as much fear as any male Death Eater. The giggling debate, with Zettel's refusal 'to tell girls that the only way to be valid human beings is to turn themselves into boys', stages the disagreement the chapter will recast as liberal versus radical feminism.

chapters.file: ch53 - More Wonderful and More Terrible than Death.md
chapters.relation: Distinguishes liberal feminism, historically grounded in Wollstonecraft, Harriet Taylor Mill, and John Stuart Mill, which holds women are autonomous persons who succeed on equal but masculine-coded terms, as in Gladstein's praise of McGonagall and Hermione, from radical feminism's analysis of the sex/gender system that forces masculine and feminine traits into rigid, ranked pairs. It reads Zettel's defense of Molly Weasley's mothering and Gallardo-C. and Smith's 'Cinderfella' interpretation, evil as 'phallic power and ambition' even in Umbridge, good as feminine-coded kindness and selflessness in Harry, as radical-feminist readings, noting thinkers from St. Gertrude to Gandhi and C.S. Lewis have likewise insisted love and compassion belong to full humanity.

Tracks love's escalation across the series as a force that overwhelms evil without competing: Lily's skin-deep sacrificial love repels Quirrell in Sorcerer's Stone, Harry spares Pettigrew out of love for Lupin and Sirius, his love for Sirius expels Voldemort's possession at the Ministry, and Dumbledore names it 'a force that is at once more wonderful and more terrible than death'. In Deathly Hallows love extends to Kreacher, Griphook, and Dobby, and culminates in Harry's astonishing plea that Voldemort 'try for some remorse', his redefinition of manhood in 'be a man', and victory through willing sacrifice and a single defensive spell rather than a duel, vindicating traditionally feminine values over hypermasculine domination.

holes.name: Alexander of Aphrodisias
holes.what: Second-century Aristotelian commentator whose On Fate argues against the view that prophecies like Apollo's to Laius cause the events they predict.
holes.why: Chapter 32 quotes Alexander at length to argue that Trelawney's prophecy revealed rather than caused Voldemort's choice of Harry, so the source of the argument needs its own slug.
